title: Functions, fibers and equivalence
description: Explain a fiber; distinguish an inverse image from an inverse; test independence of representatives.
entryCompetencies: Read set membership and compose two functions.
outcomes: Explain a fiber
distinguish an inverse image from an inverse

capstone.question: For f: Z → Z/3Z given by $f(n)=[n]_3$, describe every fiber. Does [n] modulo 3 ↦ [n²] modulo 6 define a function? Compare n=0 and n=3.
capstone.answer: Fibers are residue classes modulo 3. The proposed rule fails because 0 and 3 represent the same input but their squares are 0 and 3 modulo 6.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Operations and groups

entryCompetencies: Recognise a function and compose maps.
outcomes: Verify group axioms and distinguish order from cardinality.

capstone.question: Compare addition on Z with subtraction on Z. Derive (ab)⁻¹ and test the formula on triangle motions.
capstone.answer: Subtraction fails associativity and has no two-sided identity. Since (ab)(b⁻¹a⁻¹)=e=(b⁻¹a⁻¹)(ab), the inverse is b⁻¹a⁻¹.

completionCriteria: Demonstrate every lesson competency and solve the capstone, checking each hypothesis.

title: Subgroups, generators and cyclic structure

capstone.question: List all subgroups of C12 and determine which contain g⁴. Explain the reversed divisibility relation.
capstone.answer: The subgroups are generated by gᵈ for d=1,2,3,4,6,12. Those containing g⁴ have d dividing 4: 1,2,4. The order of gᵈ is 12/d.

title: Cosets and Lagrange

capstone.question: Partition S3 by H={e,(12)}. Can its three cosets form a quotient group with representative multiplication?
capstone.answer: The left cosets partition six elements into three pairs. H is not normal: (123)(12)(123)⁻¹=(23) is outside H. Hence the proposed quotient operation is not well-defined.

title: Homomorphisms, quotients and products
description: Prove quotient and product constructions with their exact hypotheses.
entryCompetencies: Recognise fibers and normal subgroups.

capstone.question: Use A₃ and H=⟨(12)⟩ inside S₃ to recover a product law. Why is it not direct, and why does the C₄ extension by C₂ not split?
capstone.answer: A₃ is normal of order three, H has order two, they intersect trivially and generate S₃. Conjugation by (12) inverts A₃, so S₃≅C₃⋊C₂ and the action is nontrivial. C₄ has only one subgroup of order two, its kernel, and therefore no complementary C₂.

title: Actions and orbit–stabilizer

capstone.question: For S3 acting on three letters, compute the orbit and stabilizer of 1 and the action kernel. Is a point stabilizer the kernel?
capstone.answer: The orbit is {1,2,3}; the stabilizer is {e,(23)}; the kernel is {e}. Orbit size times stabilizer size is 3·2=6. A stabilizer fixes one point, the kernel fixes every point.

capstone.question: Count binary necklaces of length 4 under rotations, including the constant necklaces.
capstone.answer: The four rotations fix 16,2,4,2 colorings. Their average is 6. Reflections are excluded; including them changes the acting group and requires another fixed-point table.

capstone.question: Prove every group of order 15 is cyclic, identifying each use of a Sylow theorem.
capstone.answer: n5 divides 3 and is 1 modulo 5, so n5=1. n3 divides 5 and is 1 modulo 3, so n3=1. The normal Sylow subgroups intersect trivially and commute; their product is C3 × C5 ≅ C15.

title: Rings, ideals and quotient rings

capstone.question: Determine the units and zero divisors of Z/12Z. Identify the kernel and image of reduction to Z/4Z.
capstone.answer: Units are 1,5,7,11. Nonzero zero divisors are 2,3,4,6,8,9,10. Reduction has kernel {0,4,8} and image Z/4Z; the first isomorphism theorem identifies the quotient by that kernel.

capstone.question: Compare x²+1 over Q, R, C and F2. Explain why a root test alone fails for degree 4.
capstone.answer: It is irreducible over Q and R, splits as (x−i)(x+i) over C, and equals (x+1)² over F2. A degree-4 polynomial can split into two quadratics without linear roots.

capstone.question: In Z localized at (3), decide whether 2 and 3 are units. Is Z Noetherian despite being infinite?
capstone.answer: 2 is a unit since its denominator is allowed; 3 is not. Every ideal of Z is principal, hence Z is Noetherian; Noetherian concerns chains of ideals, not cardinality.

capstone.question: Give a presentation and annihilator of Z/6Z as a Z-module and explain why multiplication by 2 on Z/3Z is invertible.
capstone.answer: Z/6Z has one generator with relation 6e=0 and annihilator 6Z; 0 → Z → Z → Z/6Z → 0 is exact when the first map multiplies by 6. On Z/3Z, multiplication by 2 is its own inverse, despite 2 not being a unit of Z.

capstone.question: Split the complex permutation representation of S3 on C³ into its constant line and sum-zero plane. Verify both subspaces are invariant.
capstone.answer: Coordinate permutations preserve constant vectors and coordinate sums. Their intersection is zero over C and dimensions add to 3, giving a direct sum of invariant subspaces. The projection onto constants averages the three coordinates.

capstone.question: Compute the character of the sum-zero S3 representation on identity, transposition and 3-cycle. Explain its degree and field.
capstone.answer: Over C the sum-zero plane has dimension 2. Subtract the constant character from the three-point permutation character: (3,1,0)−(1,1,1)=(2,0,−1). Maschke applies since characteristic zero does not divide 6.

capstone.question: Decompose the S3 character (5,1,−1) against trivial, sign and standard characters using class sizes 1,3,2.
capstone.answer: The inner products are 1,0,2, respectively. Thus the representation is one trivial copy plus two standard copies, of dimension 1+2·2=5.

capstone.question: Explain why two faithful factors can yield a nonfaithful external tensor product using scalar −I.
capstone.answer: On C2 take its faithful sign character; on D8 take its faithful complex two-dimensional square representation. The nonidentity pair (−1,r²) acts as (−1)⊗(−I)=I, so the product has nontrivial kernel.

capstone.question: For the order-eighteen family with $\alpha=\omega$ and $\beta=1$, identify its kernel and irreducibility.
capstone.answer: The kernel is $\langle b\rangle$ of order three. A rotation-subgroup element $a^ub^v$ acts trivially exactly when $\omega^u=1$, so u=0. An element involving s has an off-diagonal matrix and cannot act as I. The a-eigenvalues $\omega,\omega^{-1}$ are distinct, and s exchanges their lines, so the representation is irreducible but not faithful.

capstone.question: For $\theta=I+S$ on the two-dimensional swap module, compare its kernel-image decomposition over $\mathbb C$ and $\mathbb F_2$.
capstone.answer: Over C, theta has eigenvalues 0 and 2, with kernel spanned by (1,-1) and image spanned by (1,1). They are complementary invariant lines, and theta/2 is a projection. Over F2, theta is nonzero with square zero, and its kernel and image are the same line spanned by (1,1). The two roots coincide and division by two fails, so there is no kernel-image direct sum.

capstone.question: For $C_3\times C_3$, give the least faithful complex degree and the multiplicity of each irreducible in its regular module.
capstone.answer: The least faithful degree is two. Every irreducible is a linear character with image in the cube roots, so a single character cannot inject the order-nine group. Two coordinate characters have kernels with trivial intersection and form a faithful sum. The regular module contains all nine degree-one characters once, since regular multiplicity equals irreducible degree.

capstone.question: What is the rank of the degree-two isotypic projector on the eight-dimensional regular module of $D_8$, and how many irreducible copies does its image contain?
capstone.answer: The rank is four, and the image contains two copies of the degree-two irreducible. The projector is e_sigma=([1]-[r^2])/2. Its image has the four independent differences [1]-[r^2], [r]-[r^3], [s]-[r^2s], [rs]-[r^3s]. Regular multiplicity equals degree, so this is one isotypic component with two copies, rather than one irreducible copy.

capstone.question: Use the five-cube action and the spatial $C_5$ restriction to identify the dodecahedral rotation group and its trace at a positive $2\pi/5$ rotation.
capstone.answer: The coordinate action has sixty rotations. Its action on the five exhaustive inscribed cube vertex sets is faithful because common antipodal vertex pairs force a kernel rotation to fix four nonorthogonal diagonal lines, hence to be I. Its image in S5 has index two and equals A5. On spatial C5 restriction the eigenvalues are 1, zeta_5 and zeta_5 inverse, so the trace is 1+2cos(2pi/5)=phi. The other two C5 weights have multiplicity zero.

capstone.question: For C4 with lambda(r)=i and V=1 plus lambda, decompose the two squares and identify the first power containing lambda cubed.
capstone.answer: The symmetric square is 1 plus lambda plus lambda squared, and the exterior square is lambda. The third tensor power has character 1+3lambda+3lambda squared+lambda cubed, so the first occurrence of lambda cubed is exponent three. The four distinct character values give a Vandermonde guarantee using exponents zero through three.

capstone.question: In S6 let y=p3-p2 and z=vy-w as defined in the table lesson. Explain why both are actual, then calculate their values on type 3 squared and the degree of z.
capstone.answer: The equivariant pair-to-triple incidence map is injective, so a complement has actual character y. The actual tensor vy contains w once, so removing that summand gives actual z. On type (3,3), p3=2, p2=0, v=-1 and w=0, hence y=2 and z=-2. At identity z has degree 5 times 5 minus 9, equal to 16; its weighted norm is one.

capstone.question: The degree-three irreducible A4 row restricts to its normal V4 as the three nontrivial linear rows once each. Find its norm, explain equality in the index bound and identify the Clifford parameters.
capstone.answer: The squared restriction norm is 1+1+1=3, equal to the index [A4:V4]=3. Equality means the A4 character vanishes outside V4. The three distinct constituent types are permuted transitively, with common multiplicity e=1, orbit size t=3 and degree d=1, giving total degree etd=3. The abelian-subgroup degree bound is attained.

capstone.question: For the split degree-sixteen S6 row on A6, explain the two constituent degrees and solve their five-cycle entries from u+v=1 and u squared+v squared=3. Compare the self-transpose degree-twenty S7 row on A7.
capstone.answer: The index-two theorem gives two distinct A6 constituents of degree eight. The equations imply uv=-1, so u and v are (1+sqrt(5))/2 and (1-sqrt(5))/2, exchanged by swapping the two split class labels. The self-transpose S7 row is sign-invariant and restricts to two distinct A7 rows of degree ten.

capstone.question: Take R=Z, G=C4, H generated by r squared and V=Z/2 with trivial H action. Identify the induced module and r action, and explain which maps prove its tensor-coordinate decomposition.
capstone.answer: The induced module is two external copies of Z/2, indexed by 1 and r, and r swaps the copies because r squared acts trivially. Theta sends a tuple to 1 tensor v1 plus r tensor vr. Its inverse sends b tensor v to the tuple (q1(b)v,qr(b)v); right H-linearity of the q maps proves balancing, and both composites are identity. No Z-basis of V is required.

capstone.question: For H trivial in C2, V=C and a C2 module W, describe the Hom correspondence. If f multiplies V by 2 and u multiplies W by 3, check naturality and decide whether the unit is always an isomorphism.
capstone.answer: An equivariant F corresponds to v maps to F(1 tensor v), with inverse b tensor v maps to b alpha(v). Applying f and u before or after conversion gives 6 times the same corresponding map. The unit V to Res Ind V is v maps to 1 tensor v; here its target has dimension two while V has dimension one, so it is not an isomorphism. Natural inverse Hom maps do not make induction and restriction inverse functors.

capstone.question: In the D8 subgroup of S4 with r=(1234), s=(13), induce the linear character lambda(r)=-1 and lambda(s)=1. Compute its S4 values using class fusion and identify the matrix column.
capstone.answer: In S4 class order 1,2,2 squared,3,4 the induced values are (3,1,-1,0,-1). Identity gives index three; the transposition gives lambda(s)=1; double transpositions give lambda(r squared)+2lambda(rs)=1-2=-1; the three-cycle class misses D8; and the four-cycle gives lambda(r)=-1. This is the standard row v, exactly the lambda minus-plus column of the reciprocity matrix.

capstone.question: For the affine group of order twenty-one, induce lambda(a)=exp(2 pi i/7) from its order-seven normal subgroup. Give its degree, outside values, period equations and norm, then compare the index-two case of a source fixed by outside conjugation.
capstone.answer: The induced degree is three and its values vanish outside the order-seven subgroup. On its two nonidentity classes the periods satisfy u+v=-1 and uv=2, so they are (-1 plus or minus i sqrt(7))/2. Its norm is (9+3 times 2+3 times 2)/21=1, hence it is irreducible and satisfies the norm bound 1 at most index three. For a complex irreducible source fixed by outside conjugation at index two, induction instead has norm two and splits into its two distinct sign-related extensions.

capstone.question: For $G=S_3$ and $K=\langle(12)\rangle$, induce the nontrivial complex character $\sigma$ and restrict back to $K$. Compute its $G$-endomorphism dimension. Compare induction of a nontrivial cubic character from $N=A_3$, and explain which part uses complex semisimplicity.
capstone.answer: The two $K$ double cosets have intersections $K$ and $1$, so the restriction is $\sigma\oplus\mathbb CK$. Adjunction gives endomorphism dimension two, so this induced module is reducible over $\mathbb C$. For $N=A_3$, a transposition replaces a nontrivial cubic character $\zeta$ by $\zeta^{-1}\ne\zeta$, so the normal criterion gives an irreducible induced module with endomorphism dimension one. Mackey decomposition uses coordinate maps over a unital ring. Inferring irreducibility from endomorphism dimension one uses complex scalar Schur and the semisimple converse.

capstone.question: Compare the $S_6$ class of $(12345)(6)$ and the $S_7$ class of $(12345)(6)(7)$ inside $A_6$ and $A_7$. Determine splitting and the resulting class sizes, and justify the difference.
capstone.answer: Type $(5,1)$ has distinct odd lengths, centralizer order five and an $S_6$ class of size $720/5=144$. It splits into two $A_6$ classes of size 72. Type $(5,1,1)$ repeats length one and has the odd centralizer $(67)$. Its $S_7$ centralizer has order $5\cdot2=10$, and its 504 elements stay one $A_7$ class. Every fixed point must be included.

capstone.question: Use linear-first inner products. A Euclidean projection has matrix $M=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ in basis $(1,0),(1,1)$. Find its adjoint matrix. Then give the class-coordinate induction map from $H=\langle(12)\rangle$ to $S_3$ and explain the metric factors.
capstone.answer: The projection Gram matrix is $G=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$, so $[P^*]=G^{-1}M^TG=M$, although $M^T\ne M$. For class coordinates $(a,b)$ on $H$ and identity, transposition, 3-cycle coordinates on $S_3$, induction is $(a,b)\mapsto(3a,b,0)$. The Gram diagonals are $(1/2,1/2)$ and $(1/6,1/2,1/3)$, so the adjoint matrix is $D_G^{-1}R^TD_H$. Metric factors belong to both calculations.

capstone.question: For a unital $(S,R)$-bimodule $M$, a left $R$-module $V$ and a left $S$-module $W$, give both tensor-Hom maps and the Hom action. Explain why these are inverse and natural. Test whether the adjoint functors are inverse when $R=S=\mathbb C$ and $M=\mathbb C^2$.
capstone.answer: The Hom action is $(rf)(m)=f(mr)$. The maps are $T\mapsto[v\mapsto(m\mapsto T(m\otimes v))]$ and $f\mapsto[m\otimes v\mapsto f(v)(m)]$. Outer R-linearity gives $f(rv)(m)=f(v)(mr)$, the reverse balancing relation. Evaluating at $m,v$ proves both inverse identities and naturality under source precomposition and target postcomposition. For $M=\mathbb C^2$, $U(F\mathbb C)=\operatorname{End}(\mathbb C^2)$ has dimension four while $\mathbb C$ has dimension one, so the adjunction is not an inverse equivalence.

title: Tetrahedral spring modes and induction
description: Derive a complete ideal six-spring model, its symmetry decomposition, exact mass-normalized spectrum and stabilizer-induction interpretation.
entryCompetencies: Use quadratic energies and generalized eigenvalue equations.
Compute finite-group character inner products and induction multiplicities.
outcomes: Declare the free, equal-mass, unstressed central-spring assumptions.
Construct the actual polar-vector and site-permutation action of full Td.
Remove polar translations and axial rotations and recover affine mass coordinates.
Derive all six internal patterns and exact frequency families.
Use Schur with its multiplicity limits and rederive characters from a vertex stabilizer.

capstone.question: For the stated free tetrahedron with four equal masses m and six equal unstressed central springs k, derive the internal symmetry types and squared frequencies. Explain why rotations are axial, why raw shear coordinates need a different mass weight, and which conclusions follow from symmetry alone.
capstone.answer: The full displacement character is $(12,0,0,0,2)=A_1+E+T_1+2T_2$ in the class order $1,(123),(12)(34),(1234),(12)$. Translations are polar T2 and infinitesimal rotations are axial T1 because their parameter transforms by det(R)R. Removing both leaves $A_1+E+T_2$. Affine internal strains have mass matrix $4ma^2\operatorname{diag}(1,1,1,2,2,2)$ in the six raw symmetric entries. The exact energy gives squared frequencies $4k/m$ once, $k/m$ twice and $2k/m$ three times. Symmetry and single-copy Schur force the family degeneracies, while the force law and mass metric determine their values. The vertex-stabilizer tensor identity independently gives displacement multiplicities $1,0,1,1,2$.

completionCriteria: Submit correct current answers for every credited lesson competency and this unit capstone. Opening lessons, revealing proofs and reading explanations do not complete the unit.
